questions.q: A model has 32 query heads and 8 KV heads (GQA). How does its KV cache compare with full multi-head attention at the same head size?
questions.why: Cache size scales with the number of KV heads. Each group of 4 query heads shares one key and value head.

questions.q: Multi-query attention (MQA) is GQA with how many KV heads?
options: The same as the number of query heads
questions.why: MQA gives the smallest cache but can lose some quality. GQA is a middle ground between MQA and MHA.

questions.q: What does multi-head latent attention (MLA) store in the cache instead of full keys and values?
options: A compressed low-rank latent vector per token, from which keys and values are reconstructed by up-projection
questions.why: The cache holds a small latent plus a decoupled rotary key part. The up-projections can be absorbed into the query and output projections at inference time.

questions.q: Why can't rotary embeddings be applied directly to MLA's compressed latent?
options: RoPE is position-dependent, which breaks absorbing the key up-projection into the query side; MLA adds a separate small rotary key instead
questions.why: The rotation would sit between the query and the absorbed up-projection matrix, so the matrices could no longer be merged.

questions.q: In scaled dot-product attention, what is the shape of the score matrix for one head, query length q and key length k?
questions.why: Each query scores every key. Decoding has q = 1, so the score row is 1 × k.

questions.q: Why is MHA's per-token cache cost $2 \cdot n_{layers} \cdot n_{heads} \cdot d_{head} \cdot$ bytes?
options: Keys and values (the 2) are stored for every layer and head
Only the last layer is cached
questions.why: For a 32-layer model with 32 heads of size 128 in fp16, that is 2·32·32·128·2 bytes ≈ 0.5 MB per token.

questions.q: Converting an MHA checkpoint to GQA is commonly done how?
options: Delete all but one head without further training
Mean-pool the key and value heads within each group, then fine-tune briefly
questions.why: This "uptraining" recovers most of the quality at a small fraction of the original pretraining compute.

questions.q: Why does reducing KV heads speed up decoding more than prefill?
options: Decoding is limited by reading the KV cache, so fewer bytes per token directly cuts step time; prefill is mostly compute-bound
questions.why: Prefill processes many tokens at once and is dominated by matmuls. Each decode step rereads the whole cache for one new token.

questions.q: During decoding, how is the rotary position for the new token chosen?
options: Its absolute index in the sequence, which equals the current cache length
questions.why: Cached keys were rotated at their own positions. Using the wrong offset for the new token breaks the relative-position property.

questions.q: What does FlashAttention change about attention's result?
options: It approximates attention with a low-rank method
Nothing mathematically; it reorders computation to avoid materialising the full score matrix
questions.why: It is exact up to floating-point rounding. The speedup comes from cutting memory traffic, not FLOPs.

questions.q: In the order temperature → top-k → top-p, what does top-k = 50 do after temperature scaling?
options: Keeps the 50 highest-probability tokens and renormalises before applying top-p
questions.why: The order of these filters changes the result, so serving systems define it explicitly.

questions.q: In a top-2 sparse MoE layer, what does each token's output combine?
options: The outputs of all experts, averaged
The outputs of its 2 selected experts, weighted by their (often renormalised) router probabilities
questions.why: Compute per token is about that of 2 FFNs, while total parameters scale with the number of experts.

questions.q: Why is an auxiliary load-balancing loss (or an equivalent bias) used in MoE training?
options: Without it, the router tends to send most tokens to a few experts, wasting capacity and overflowing their buffers
To reduce the number of experts
questions.why: A common form multiplies each expert's token fraction by its mean router probability, summed over experts.

questions.q: What does token dispatch in an MoE layer do?
options: Sends every token to every expert
Groups tokens by their chosen expert so each expert runs one batched matmul, then scatters outputs back in the original order
questions.why: Permute, compute and un-permute are the main data-movement steps. With expert parallelism they become all-to-all communications.

questions.q: What is an expert's capacity factor?
options: The number of parameters in an expert
The number of layers per expert
A multiplier on the average tokens per expert that sets its buffer size; tokens beyond it are dropped or rerouted
questions.why: Capacity = factor × tokens × k / experts. A higher factor drops fewer tokens but wastes memory and compute on padding.

questions.q: Why does top-p sampling need a sort, or an equivalent selection?
options: It doesn't; it thresholds each probability independently
It must find the smallest set of highest-probability tokens whose cumulative mass reaches p
questions.why: Over a vocabulary of 100k+ tokens this is a noticeable cost, and kernels often use partial sorts or radix selection.

questions.q: Why does a KV cache speed up autoregressive generation?
options: Keys and values of earlier tokens are computed once and reused, so each step processes only the new token
questions.why: Without a cache each step recomputes the whole prefix, making generation quadratic in compute.

questions.q: A model has 40 layers, 8 KV heads of size 128, in fp16. How many bytes of KV cache does one token use?
questions.why: 2 (K and V) · 40 · 8 · 128 · 2 bytes = 163,840 bytes, about 160 KB per token.

questions.q: What problem does PagedAttention solve?
options: Fragmentation and over-reservation from allocating each request's maximum-length cache contiguously
questions.why: The cache is split into fixed-size blocks mapped through a block table, like virtual memory pages, so memory is allocated as sequences grow.

questions.q: How does prefix caching save compute?
options: Requests sharing a prompt prefix (such as a system prompt) reuse the cached KV blocks for that prefix instead of recomputing them
questions.why: Matching is usually done per full block with hashes of the token IDs, often in a radix tree.

questions.q: In speculative decoding, what does the target model do with the draft's k proposed tokens?
options: Uses them only as training data
Scores all of them in one forward pass and accepts a prefix using a rejection-sampling rule that preserves its own distribution
Generates k tokens itself one by one
questions.why: Token i is accepted with probability min(1, p/q). On the first rejection, a replacement is sampled from the normalised residual max(0, p - q).

questions.q: When does speculative decoding give the biggest speedup?
options: When the draft model is larger than the target
When the draft model is much cheaper and its tokens are frequently accepted
When the batch is very large and compute-bound
questions.why: At large batch the target is already compute-bound, so verifying extra tokens costs real FLOPs and the gain shrinks.

questions.q: Why is the KV cache often the limit on batch size, rather than the weights?
options: Weights are stored on the CPU
The cache is shared between requests
Cache memory grows with batch × sequence length, while the weights are a fixed cost shared by all requests
questions.why: At long contexts, cache memory per request can exceed the size of the model.

questions.q: What happens to throughput if the KV cache doesn't fit and requests must be preempted?
options: Preempted requests must have their cache swapped out or recomputed, which wastes time and lowers throughput
The model's weights are evicted instead
questions.why: Schedulers try to admit only as many requests as the free block pool can support.

questions.q: In symmetric int8 quantisation with scale s = max|x|/127, how is a value dequantised?
questions.why: Symmetric quantisation has no zero point, so 0 maps exactly to 0. Asymmetric schemes add a zero point for skewed ranges.

questions.q: Why does per-channel weight quantisation usually beat per-tensor?
options: It removes the need for scales
Each output channel gets its own scale, so channels with small weights aren't crushed by one large outlier elsewhere
questions.why: The extra storage is one scale per channel, which is negligible next to the weights.

questions.q: In group-wise int4 quantisation with group size 128, what is stored per group?
options: One scale for the whole matrix
A full-precision copy of the group
A scale (and sometimes a zero point) shared by 128 consecutive weights
questions.why: Smaller groups track local ranges better but add more metadata. 128 is a common compromise.

questions.q: Why does weight-only quantisation speed up decoding even though matmuls still run in 16-bit?
options: Decoding is memory-bound on reading weights, and 4-bit weights cut those bytes by about 4×
It reduces the number of layers
questions.why: Weights are dequantised on the fly inside the kernel. The saving is in bytes moved, not FLOPs.

questions.q: What does block-wise FP8 quantisation use a scale per block for?
options: To keep each block's values within FP8's narrow range, limiting the damage from outliers
questions.why: FP8 E4M3 has few mantissa bits and a limited range. Per-block scales such as 128×128 keep large and small regions accurate.

questions.q: In the roofline model, when is a kernel memory-bound?
options: When its arithmetic intensity is below the GPU's peak FLOP/s divided by its memory bandwidth
When it uses more than half the memory
questions.why: Below that ridge point, attainable performance is bandwidth × intensity, not peak compute.

questions.q: Why is prefill typically compute-bound while decode at small batch is memory-bound?
options: Prefill multiplies each loaded weight by many tokens; decode multiplies each weight by only a few
questions.why: Arithmetic intensity of a matmul scales with the number of tokens processed per weight load.

questions.q: A 70B-parameter model in fp16 is decoded at batch 1 on a GPU with 3 TB/s bandwidth. Roughly what is the best possible time per token?
questions.why: The weights are 140 GB, and 140 GB ÷ 3 TB/s ≈ 47 ms, ignoring the KV cache. Real systems split the model across GPUs to fit it and go faster.

questions.q: Why report p99 latency and not just the mean?
options: p99 is always lower than the mean
Tail latency determines the worst experience many users see, and the mean hides it
The mean can't be computed for latencies
questions.why: A service with a 100 ms mean can still have a 2 s p99, and requests that fan out across many calls hit the tail often.

questions.q: What does TTFT measure?
options: Time from receiving a request to emitting its first output token, mostly queueing plus prefill
Tokens per second across all users
questions.why: TTFT is what users notice as responsiveness. TPOT or ITL measures how quickly the rest of the text streams.

questions.q: How is TPOT (time per output token) usually computed for one request?
questions.why: It averages the decode-phase gaps. Inter-token latency (ITL) looks at each gap individually and so shows jitter.

questions.q: What is the main drawback of static (request-level) batching for LLMs?
options: The batch runs until its longest request finishes, so slots of finished requests sit idle
It can't batch more than two requests
questions.why: Generation lengths vary widely, so many slots finish early and wait.

questions.q: What does continuous batching do?
options: Runs one request at a time
Waits for a fixed number of requests before starting
Schedules at the iteration level, adding new requests and removing finished ones at every decode step
questions.why: This keeps the GPU busy and is a major reason for the throughput of modern serving engines.

questions.q: What problem does chunked prefill address?
options: A long prompt's prefill would stall decode steps for other requests; splitting it into chunks interleaves them
questions.why: Each iteration mixes a prefill chunk with ongoing decodes, smoothing inter-token latency at a small cost to TTFT.

questions.q: In dynamic batching for a classic model server, what two knobs control the batcher?
options: Maximum batch size and maximum wait time before a partial batch is sent
questions.why: Waiting longer fills bigger batches and raises throughput, but adds queueing delay to every request in the batch.

questions.q: How does throughput usually change as batch size grows in LLM decoding?
options: It rises roughly linearly while memory-bound, then flattens once the GPU becomes compute-bound or memory runs out
questions.why: Per-request latency grows as batches get larger, so serving picks the largest batch that still meets the latency target.

questions.q: A 70B model in bf16 must fit on 80 GB GPUs, with 20% of memory reserved for KV cache and overhead. What is the minimum number of GPUs?
questions.why: Weights are 140 GB, and each GPU has 64 GB usable, so 140/64 ≈ 2.2 rounds up to 3. In practice tensor parallelism prefers 4 because head counts divide evenly.

questions.q: In Megatron-style tensor parallelism of an MLP, where is communication needed?
options: One all-reduce after the row-parallel second matmul in the forward pass
Before the first matmul only, with a broadcast of the weights
questions.why: The first matmul splits columns and the second splits rows, so partial outputs are summed once.

questions.q: Why is tensor parallelism usually kept within one node?
options: Its all-reduces happen every layer and need the high bandwidth of intra-node links like NVLink
It can't span nodes at all
questions.why: Across nodes, pipeline or expert parallelism tolerates the lower bandwidth better.

questions.q: In expert parallelism, what communication pattern moves tokens to their experts?
questions.why: Each GPU sends each token to the GPU holding its chosen expert and receives results back with a second all-to-all.

questions.q: What is disaggregated prefill and decode serving?
options: Running both phases on the CPU
Running prefill and decode on separate GPU pools and transferring the KV cache between them
Splitting a model's layers across GPUs
questions.why: The phases have different bottlenecks (compute versus bandwidth), so separating them lets each pool be sized and tuned independently.

questions.q: What is the main cost of disaggregation?
options: Moving each request's KV cache from the prefill pool to the decode pool
questions.why: For long prompts the cache can be gigabytes, so fast interconnects and overlapping transfer with compute matter.

questions.q: When choosing a serving configuration under a latency SLO, what is usually maximised?
options: Largest possible batch regardless of latency
Throughput (or tokens per dollar) among configurations whose p95 or p99 latency meets the target
Lowest possible latency at any cost
questions.why: Sweep batch size, parallelism and quantisation, discard configurations that miss the SLO, and pick the cheapest of the rest.

questions.q: Why can adding more GPUs with tensor parallelism stop improving decode latency?
options: GPUs slow each other down by heating
Per-GPU work shrinks while all-reduce communication per layer stays roughly constant, so communication dominates
questions.why: Past a point, each layer's compute is too small to hide the latency of the collective.
